transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~38 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Sofia (CTO - Brighton), Devon (ML Eng), Asha (Security), Evan (Product)

Summary: quick hosted API walkthrough focusing on chat/text generation basics: streaming, request params, retries/ idempotency, Console overview and Redwood Optimize tips for batching/caching. Customer interested in latency targets and data residency.

Topics: hosted API, streaming responses, temperature/top_p/max_tokens, retries and idempotency tokens, rate limits, SDK examples, Console demo, Optimize suggestions (batching/caching/quantization recs), security (SOC2, KMS), POC next steps.

00:00 Maya (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we have about 35-40 minutes today, main goal is a quick hosted API demo — chat and text generation basics, show streaming and params, and then Liam will do the more technical bits around retries and SDK samples.
00:18 Sofia (CTO): thanks, Maya. quick note: our timeline is 6-8 weeks for a pilot, but security sign-off is a hard blocker. Asha here will lead that.
00:28 Asha (Security): yeah, we'll need SOC2 report, SAML/SSO integration notes, and KMS/HSM options for key management. also curious about data retention and logs.
00:40 Maya: great, we have all that. i'll send the security pack after the call. Liam, quick intro?
00:45 Liam (SE): yeah hi, i'm Liam, i'll run the demo — i'll start with the REST and SDK calls for chat generation, then show streaming, and finish with retry/backoff and idempotency token patterns.
01:05 Liam (SE): ok jumping in — basic chat request: you post messages array, system/user/assistant roles, set model field, and then we have params: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequence. example — temperature 0.2 for deterministic, 0.8 for creative.
01:32 Devon (ML Eng): do you have per-request token limits? we mostly do short answers 50-150 tokens but sometimes larger summaries.
01:40 Liam (SE): yes model and region determine limits; for hosted we surface per-model token limits and per-route quotas. we'll share a docs link and i'll include the exact numbers in the benchmark sheet.
02:02 Liam (SE): streaming demo now — i'm going to call the SDK with streaming:on, you should see incremental deltas (like delta tokens) back to client. (link to demo notebook: https://redwood.example.com/demo/streaming-chat)
02:24 02:24 Liam (SE):  [screen share sound]  — typing… the stream sends several small chunks, client can render progressively, good for chat UI or token-by-token display. note: network glitches can drop connections — we recommend an idempotency token pattern so the server can resume or clients can safely retry.
03:00 Evan (Product): what about latency? our product needs median token latency under 60ms for short responses.
03:10 Liam: for short responses we often hit 20-40ms per token on our preferred low-latency variants; for long form, sampling increases time. there are tradeoffs: lower temperature and smaller context tends to be faster. also our routing and model variants can optimize for latency vs cost.
03:36 Sofia: and cost — how do you price tokens for hosted? is there burst pricing?
03:42 Maya: hosted is usage-based per token and per-embedding units; we show pre and post-token counts in console. burst is supported up to a quota, Dedicated is for predictable throughput. i'll attach the rate card.
04:00 Liam: demoing params — temperature, top_p, presence_penalty; show examples where small param tweaks change hallucination behavior. also show max_tokens and truncation behavior.
05:10 Liam: now retries — we recommend exponential backoff with jitter and client-side idempotency keys for safety. server-side we do automatic retries for internal transient errors but client should handle 429s and 5xx with backoff. sample code in the repo shows 3 retries by default, with 200-500ms base backoff.
05:42 Devon: do you expose the retry-after header for rate limits?
05:45 Liam: yes we return Retry-After on 429s, and our SDK surfaces it. also we include a request id in response headers for correlation with logs.
06:02 Asha: audit logs — can we get per-request logs for compliance?
06:07 Maya: yes, Audit logs are available in Redwood Console for Dedicated and Private; for hosted we provide configurable retention and logs for enterprise plans. we also have an export hook for SIEM.
06:25 Liam: quick Console walkthrough — showing per-route dashboards: token cost, latency percentiles, error rates. here we flag high latency requests and can drill into example prompts (redacted) and stack traces. (note: console screenshot link shared)
07:00 Liam: Optimize tips — automatic batching suggestions, KV cache/prefix caching for repeated prompts, and quantization recommendations for self-hosted variants. for hosted we do prefix caching to reduce cost when there are repeated beginnings.
07:30 Evan: can you explain prefix caching?
07:33 Liam: sure — if many requests share common prompt prefixes, we cache the KV cache for that prefix so subsequent requests don't recompute early layers; reduces per-token compute. we also recommend request-level caching for reranking or deterministic responses.
08:02 Devon: about batching — our backend aggregates hundreds of tiny requests, will Redwood do request coalescing?
08:10 Liam: hosted runtime does continuous batching where it makes sense but it's workload-dependent; Optimize can recommend batch sizes and concurrency settings. for tight-latency apps you can pin smaller batch windows.
08:32 Sofia: security again — data residency. we have EU customers, need GDPR assurances and logs staying in EU region.
08:40 Maya: we support regional endpoints and data residency controls for enterprise plans. we'll include regional SLA and data flow diagrams in the pack.
09:00 Asha: key management — do you support customer-managed keys?
09:05 Liam: yes, for Dedicated and Private we support KMS/HSM integrations. hosted customers on enterprise plan can request CMK support — details in security pack.
09:22 Devon: on retries/resuming streams — if client disconnects mid-stream, can we resume?
09:28 Liam: we don't resume streams at level of token offsets today; recommended pattern is to use idempotency and re-request with resume hints. for most clients we re-generate from the last committed assistant message. resumption is on roadmap but not guaranteed for hosted.
10:00 Evan: what about SDKs — do you have official Node and Python libs with streaming?
10:05 Liam: yes official SDKs include streaming helpers, examples for websockets and HTTP chunked streams. i'll share the sample repo.
10:25 Liam: quick demo of sample Node code (shows streaming and reconnect logic). code has backoff, idempotency token generation sample.
11:40 Sofia: how deterministic can responses be? we have a use-case for deterministic templated replies.
11:48 Liam: lower temp, top_p near 0.0, and set a deterministic seed if you use our deterministic sampling variants — note not all models support seeding. also use shorter max_tokens and explicit stop sequences.
12:15 Devon: fine-tuning vs prompts — we don't want to fine-tune now, mostly prompt engineering + system messages.
12:22 Liam: that works. we also provide eval tooling to monitor prompt drift and quality regressions. Optimize can run quality checks against test prompts and alert on regressions.
13:00 Maya: quick note about cost controls — per-route quotas, token caps in console, throttling rules.
13:12 Evan: do you support webhooks for async job completions?
13:16 Liam: yes, for long-running batch jobs or embedding jobs we have async endpoints and webhook callbacks.
13:32 Asha: legal and procurement — we need a data processing addendum and standard contract redline.
13:38 Maya: procurement team will coordinate, i'll attach DPA template and sample SOW.
13:45 Liam: i'm going to show a brief benchmark we ran — numbers across variants: low-latency model median token latency ~30ms, cost ~X per 1k tokens (will share exact in sheet). (shared benchmark link)
14:10 Devon: could you run a quick POC against a small representative dataset? we want to measure latency from our infra location and typical prompt shapes.
14:17 Maya: yes, we recommend a short POC: 1-2 week pilot with sample prompts. Liam will help scope.
14:30 Liam: POC scoping ideas: 1) run 1k sample prompts from your traffic, 2) measure p50/p95 latencies and token counts, 3) test streaming UX and client retry behavior, 4) evaluate cost with Optimize recommendations.
15:00 Sofia: team availability — we'll need SE time and security docs. also product wants to validate UX.
15:10 Maya: ok recap will include who does what.
15:20 Liam: closing demo notes — common pitfalls: not handling 429s, relying on unlimited token contexts, and not instrumenting token usage. we provide SDK telemetry hooks to help.
15:40 Maya: any final q's?
15:45 Evan: what are next steps on scheduling POC?
15:48 Maya: we'll propose a POC plan in an email and offer two windows next week for the scoping call.
15:55 Sofia: thanks everyone.
16:00 Asha: thanks — we'll review security pack and come back with required items.
